abstract: Cell migration plays a central role in development, ensuring cells reach their correct destinations. Many migratory cell types require interaction with the extracellular matrix (ECM) to generate traction. While the basal ECM (bECM) is well known for its role in cell motility, the apical ECM (aECM) has mostly been shown to provide structural and mechanical support during morphogenesis and remains less understood. In Drosophila, the aECM is primarily composed of the giant protein Dumpy (Dpy), which interacts with the Zona Pellucida (ZP) domain protein Piopio (Pio). In this study, we elucidate the role of the aECM in the formation of the adult abdominal epidermis of Drosophila. During this process, the larval epithelial cells (LECs) transition from a stationary to a mobile state, in which they migrate directionally, before apically constricting and undergoing apoptosis. Using in vivo 4D microscopy, we examined the role of the aECM in the dynamic behaviour of the LECs. Initially, a layer of Dpy and Pio is located apically to the stationary LECs. As migration begins, the LECs leave behind this early layer while depositing an additional, morphologically distinct layer of Dpy. Knock-down of Dpy or Pio leads to the detachment of stationary LECs from the early layer and, subsequently, to impaired LEC migration. Our results reveal that the aECM transitions from acting as an anchoring scaffold to supporting cell migration. This functional change is closely linked to the change in LEC behaviour. Together, these findings identify the aECM as a substrate for cell migration and highlight a dynamic role of the aECM during morphogenesis.
